Medicine 05.question: ১) Massive proteinuria occurs in......?
Medicine 05.exp:
Massive proteinuria is a hallmark of nephrotic syndrome, classically defined as urinary protein loss of >3–3.5 g/day in adults. It results from increased glomerular permeability to plasma proteins.

The other options do not characteristically produce massive proteinuria:

  • AGN: Usually causes hematuria with variable, generally non-nephrotic proteinuria.

  • UTI: May cause mild proteinuria but not massive protein loss.

  • AKI: Refers to acute deterioration of renal function and is not itself defined by heavy proteinuria.

High-yield Nephrotic syndrome recall:

  • Massive proteinuria

  • Hypoalbuminemia

  • Generalized edema

  • Hyperlipidemia

  • Lipiduria

Exam pearl: Massive proteinuria → think nephrotic syndrome.

Medicine 05.question: ২) What is the cause of CRF with normal sized kidney?
Medicine 05.exp:
Diabetic nephropathy is a common cause of chronic renal failure (CRF) with normal-sized or enlarged kidneys. In contrast, many other chronic renal diseases cause small, shrunken kidneys due to chronic scarring.

  • PCKD: Enlarged kidneys with multiple cysts

  • Amyloidosis: Kidneys are often enlarged, especially early in the disease

  • Hydronephrosis: Typically causes enlargement/dilatation of the collecting system rather than the classic normal-sized kidney pattern

High-yield CRF kidney size recall:

  • Normal/large kidneys: Diabetes mellitus, amyloidosis, polycystic kidney disease, infiltrative diseases

  • Small kidneys: Chronic glomerulonephritis, chronic pyelonephritis, reflux nephropathy

Exam pearl: CRF + normal/large kidneys → think diabetes mellitus, amyloidosis, or infiltrative disease.

Medicine 05.question: ৩) What is the cause of sodium & water depletion due to renal loss?
Medicine 05.exp:
Diuretic therapy causes renal loss of sodium and water by increasing urinary excretion. Loop and thiazide diuretics are common causes of hypovolemia and hyponatremia when the losses are significant.

The other options cause sodium and water loss mainly through extrarenal routes:

  • Vomiting → gastrointestinal loss

  • Pancreatitis → third-space/fluid sequestration

  • Burns → loss through damaged skin and third spacing

High-yield Sodium & water depletion recall:

  • Renal loss: Diuretics, adrenal insufficiency, salt-wasting nephropathy

  • GI loss: Vomiting, diarrhea

  • Skin loss: Burns, excessive sweating

  • Third spacing: Pancreatitis, peritonitis

Exam pearl: Sodium + water depletion due to renal loss → think diuretics.

Medicine 05.question: ৪) N-Acetylcysteine is used as antidote for which poisoning?
Medicine 05.exp:
N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is the specific antidote for paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning. It replenishes hepatic glutathione, allowing detoxification of the toxic metabolite NAPQI and preventing or reducing hepatic injury.

  • Benzodiazepine poisoning → Flumazenil in selected cases

  • Organophosphorus compound (OPC) poisoning → Atropine + pralidoxime

  • Barbiturate poisoning → supportive management; urinary alkalinization may be used for phenobarbital in selected cases

High-yield Antidotes recall:

  • Paracetamol → N-acetylcysteine

  • Benzodiazepines → Flumazenil

  • OPC → Atropine + Pralidoxime

  • Opioids → Naloxone

Exam pearl: Paracetamol overdose → NAC → replenishes glutathione → detoxifies NAPQI.

Medicine 05.question: ৫) Which antihypertensive is usually regarded as drug of choice in CKD?
Medicine 05.exp:
ACE inhibitors are generally regarded as the preferred antihypertensive agents in chronic kidney disease (CKD), particularly when albuminuria/proteinuria is present. They reduce intraglomerular pressure and decrease proteinuria, thereby providing renal protection in addition to BP control.

High-yield CKD antihypertensive recall:

  • ACE inhibitor/ARB: Preferred when albuminuria is present

  • ↓ Efferent arteriolar constriction → ↓ intraglomerular pressure

  • ↓ Proteinuria → renal protective effect

  • Monitor serum creatinine and potassium after initiation

Exam pearl: CKD + proteinuria → ACE inhibitor or ARB is the classic drug of choice.

Medicine 05.question: ৬) Which is a sign of hypovolemia?
Medicine 05.exp:
Low JVP (jugular venous pressure) is a clinical sign of hypovolemia, reflecting reduced intravascular volume and decreased venous return to the heart.

The other options suggest fluid overload:

  • Peripheral oedema → fluid accumulation

  • Ascites → fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity

  • Crepitations → may indicate pulmonary oedema

High-yield Hypovolemia signs recall:

  • Low JVP

  • Tachycardia

  • Postural hypotension

  • Cold peripheries

  • Reduced urine output

  • Dry mucous membranes

Exam pearl: Hypovolemia → low JVP + tachycardia + postural hypotension.

Medicine 05.question: ৭) Which is a feature of nicotinic effect of OPC poisoning?
Medicine 05.exp:
In organophosphorus compound (OPC) poisoning, excessive acetylcholine stimulates nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction, producing muscle fasciculations followed by muscle weakness and paralysis.

  • Constriction of pupil → muscarinic effect

  • Urinary and faecal incontinence → muscarinic effect

  • Breathlessness → may occur due to both muscarinic bronchorrhea/bronchospasm and nicotinic respiratory muscle weakness, but is not the best specific answer here.

High-yield OPC poisoning recall:

  • Muscarinic: salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhoea, bronchorrhea, miosis

  • Nicotinic: fasciculations, muscle weakness, paralysis, hypertension/tachycardia may occur

  • CNS: confusion, seizures, coma

Exam pearl: OPC nicotinic effect → fasciculations → muscle weakness → paralysis.

Medicine 05.question: ৮) What is the most common cause of dysuria?
Medicine 05.exp:
Cystitis, most commonly caused by a bacterial urinary tract infection, is the most common cause of dysuria, particularly in women. Typical symptoms include burning micturition, urinary frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort.

  • Urethritis → commonly associated with sexually transmitted infections.

  • Prostatitis → dysuria may occur with pelvic/perineal pain and systemic symptoms.

  • Bladder outflow obstruction → mainly causes hesitancy, weak stream, and incomplete emptying.

High-yield Dysuria recall:

  • Most common cause → UTI/cystitis

  • Common associated symptoms → frequency + urgency + suprapubic pain

  • Dysuria + urethral discharge → think urethritis/STI

Exam pearl: Dysuria + frequency + urgency → think cystitis.

Medicine 05.question: ৯) Which electrolyte imbalance does not usually occur after diarrhoea?
Medicine 05.exp:
Diarrhoea typically causes metabolic acidosis, not metabolic alkalosis, because intestinal fluid contains significant amounts of bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻). Loss of bicarbonate leads to hyperchloremic normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

Diarrhoea can also cause hyponatremia and hypokalemia due to gastrointestinal losses.

High-yield Diarrhoea electrolyte disturbance recall:

  • Hypokalemia → potassium loss

  • Hyponatremia → sodium and water loss/replacement with hypotonic fluids

  • Metabolic acidosis → bicarbonate loss

  • Metabolic alkalosis → classically associated with vomiting, not diarrhoea

Exam pearl: Diarrhoea → HCO₃⁻ loss → metabolic acidosis; vomiting → H⁺ loss → metabolic alkalosis.

Medicine 05.question: ১০) Intermediate syndrome usually occurs after about....... hours of OPC poisoning?
Medicine 05.exp:
Intermediate syndrome (IMS) in organophosphorus compound (OPC) poisoning typically develops 24–96 hours after the acute cholinergic phase, with around 48 hours being the classic exam answer. It is characterized by proximal muscle weakness, neck flexor weakness, cranial nerve weakness, and respiratory muscle weakness.

High-yield OPC poisoning recall:

  • Acute cholinergic syndrome: occurs early

  • Intermediate syndrome: usually 24–96 hours, classically ~48 hours

  • Delayed neuropathy: develops after 1–3 weeks

  • IMS may cause respiratory failure due to respiratory muscle weakness.

Exam pearl: OPC poisoning → Intermediate syndrome ≈ 48 hours → proximal + respiratory muscle weakness.

Medicine 05.question: ১১) Which is usually the initial symptom of CKD?
Medicine 05.exp:
Nocturia is often an early symptom of chronic kidney disease (CKD) because the kidneys gradually lose their ability to concentrate urine. This results in increased urine production at night.

  • Hematuria → may occur depending on the underlying renal disease, but is not the usual initial symptom of CKD.

  • Tiredness → generally becomes prominent with more advanced CKD, particularly due to anemia and uremia.

  • Vomiting → usually indicates advanced uremia.

High-yield CKD early features recall:

  • Nocturia

  • Polyuria due to impaired concentrating ability

  • Later → fatigue, pruritus, anorexia, nausea/vomiting

  • Advanced disease → uremic symptoms

Exam pearl: Early CKD → impaired concentrating ability → nocturia.

Medicine 05.question: ১২) Which fluid is usually given in vomiting ?
Medicine 05.exp:
Normal saline (0.9% NaCl) is commonly used for fluid replacement in significant vomiting because vomiting causes loss of water, sodium, chloride, and hydrogen ions, leading to hypovolemia and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. NS helps restore intravascular volume and chloride.

  • 5% dextrose: Provides free water after glucose metabolism but is not appropriate for initial volume resuscitation.

  • 5% DNS: Not the usual first choice for volume replacement.

  • Cholera saline: Specifically formulated for cholera-associated dehydration and is not routinely required for ordinary vomiting.

High-yield Vomiting fluid management recall:

  • Vomiting → volume depletion + chloride loss

  • Initial IV fluid → 0.9% normal saline

  • Severe hypokalemia → add potassium after confirming adequate urine output

Exam pearl: Vomiting → chloride and volume loss → replace with normal saline.

Medicine 05.question: ১৩) Which is Benzodiazepine antagonist?
Medicine 05.exp:
Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine binding site on the GABA-A receptor and can reverse the sedative effects of benzodiazepines.

  • Atropine → muscarinic antagonist; used in organophosphate poisoning

  • Pralidoxime → reactivates acetylcholinesterase; used in organophosphate poisoning

  • N-acetylcysteine (NAC) → antidote for paracetamol poisoning

High-yield Antidotes recall:

  • Benzodiazepines → Flumazenil

  • Paracetamol → N-acetylcysteine

  • Organophosphates → Atropine + Pralidoxime

  • Opioids → Naloxone

Exam pearl: Benzodiazepine antagonist = Flumazenil.

Medicine 05.question: ১৪) Which is not a feature of ARF?
Medicine 05.exp:
Renal osteodystrophy is a complication of chronic kidney disease (CKD), resulting from long-standing disturbances in calcium, phosphate, vitamin D metabolism, and secondary hyperparathyroidism. It is not a feature of acute renal failure (ARF/AKI).

The other options are consistent with acute renal failure:

  • Develops over hours to days (rather than typically weeks)

  • Often reversible if the underlying cause is treated

  • Oliguria may occur, although some patients have non-oliguric AKI

High-yield ARF vs CKD recall:

  • AKI/ARF: rapid onset, potentially reversible, oliguria may occur

  • CKD: progressive and usually irreversible, anemia, renal osteodystrophy, small kidneys in many causes

Exam pearl: Renal osteodystrophy = chronic kidney disease, not acute renal failure.

Medicine 05.question: ১৫) Which is a cause of hypovolemic hyponatremia?
Medicine 05.exp:
Burns can cause hypovolemic hyponatremia due to substantial loss of both water and sodium through damaged skin and capillary leakage. The resulting reduction in extracellular fluid volume activates ADH, which promotes water retention and can worsen hyponatremia.

  • SIADH → euvolemic hyponatremia

  • CCF (congestive cardiac failure) → hypervolemic hyponatremia

  • CLD (chronic liver disease/cirrhosis) → hypervolemic hyponatremia

High-yield Hyponatremia classification recall:

  • Hypovolemic: burns, vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics

  • Euvolemic: SIADH, hypothyroidism, glucocorticoid deficiency

  • Hypervolemic: CCF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, advanced CKD

Exam pearl: Hyponatremia + volume depletion → think burns, GI loss, or diuretics.

Medicine 05.question: ১৬) Which is primary glomerular cause of Nephrotic syndrome?
Medicine 05.exp:
Minimal change disease (MCD) is a primary glomerular disease and a classic cause of nephrotic syndrome, especially in children. It causes heavy proteinuria due to increased glomerular permeability, with normal light microscopy and diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement on electron microscopy.

  • DM → secondary glomerular cause

  • SLE → secondary glomerular cause

  • HIV → secondary cause, classically associated with collapsing FSGS

High-yield Nephrotic syndrome recall:

  • Primary: Minimal change disease, FSGS, membranous nephropathy

  • Secondary: Diabetes mellitus, SLE, amyloidosis, HIV

  • MCD → most common nephrotic syndrome in children

Exam pearl: Nephrotic syndrome + primary glomerular disease → think Minimal change disease.

Medicine 05.question: ১৭) What is the sodium content of 1L NS?
Medicine 05.exp:
0.9% Normal Saline (NS) contains 154 mmol/L of sodium (Na⁺) and 154 mmol/L of chloride (Cl⁻). Therefore, the total osmolarity is approximately 308 mOsm/L, making it slightly hyperosmolar compared with plasma.

High-yield IV fluid recall:

  • 0.9% NS: Na⁺ 154 mmol/L, Cl⁻ 154 mmol/L

  • Total osmolarity: ~308 mOsm/L

  • Commonly used for volume resuscitation and extracellular fluid replacement

Exam pearl: 1 L of 0.9% NS = 154 mmol Na⁺ + 154 mmol Cl⁻.

Medicine 05.question: ১৮) Which one is the common organism for honeymoon cystitis?
Medicine 05.exp:
Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a common cause of acute uncomplicated cystitis in sexually active young women, classically called “honeymoon cystitis.” It is the second most common cause of community-acquired UTI after E. coli in this group.

High-yield UTI organism recall:

  • Most common UTI overall: E. coli

  • Honeymoon cystitis: S. saprophyticus

  • Pseudomonas: complicated/hospital-acquired UTI

  • Proteus: associated with urease production and struvite stones

Exam pearl: Young sexually active woman + cystitis = think S. saprophyticus.

Medicine 05.question: ১৯) Which is used for correction of moderate hyponatremia?
Medicine 05.exp:
0.9% NaCl (normal saline) is commonly used to correct moderate hypovolemic hyponatremia, because it restores both intravascular volume and sodium. The choice of fluid depends on the severity, symptoms, and volume status.

  • 3% NaCl: Reserved mainly for severe or symptomatic hyponatremia, particularly with neurological symptoms.

  • Oral table salt: May be used in selected chronic cases but is not the standard answer for acute volume-depleted hyponatremia.

  • Coconut water: Not appropriate for correcting significant hyponatremia.

High-yield Hyponatremia treatment recall:

  • Hypovolemic hyponatremia → 0.9% NaCl

  • Severe symptomatic hyponatremia → 3% hypertonic saline

  • Correct sodium carefully to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome.

Exam pearl: Hypovolemic moderate hyponatremia → 0.9% NaCl; severe symptomatic → 3% NaCl.

Medicine 05.question: ২০) Which is a cardinal presentation of AGN?
Medicine 05.exp:
Hematuria is a cardinal feature of acute glomerulonephritis (AGN). It is often accompanied by oliguria, edema, hypertension, and impaired renal function. Urine microscopy typically shows dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts, indicating glomerular bleeding.

  • Polyuria → not typical; oliguria is more common.

  • Hypotension → hypertension is more characteristic.

  • Hyperlipidemia → classically associated with nephrotic syndrome.

High-yield AGN presentation recall:

  • Hematuria

  • Edema

  • Hypertension

  • Oliguria

  • ↑ Serum creatinine

  • RBC casts

Exam pearl: AGN = hematuria + edema + hypertension + oliguria.

Medicine 05.question: ২১) What is the cause of euvolemic hypernatremia?
Medicine 05.exp:
Diabetes insipidus (DI) can cause euvolemic hypernatremia when the patient has adequate access to water and compensates for excessive free-water loss by drinking. In DI, deficiency of ADH (central DI) or renal resistance to ADH (nephrogenic DI) causes loss of free water, leading to increased serum sodium.

  • Diuretic therapy → typically causes hypovolemic sodium loss.

  • Glycosuria → causes osmotic diuresis and usually contributes to volume depletion.

  • CRF → commonly causes impaired water and electrolyte regulation but is not the classic cause of euvolemic hypernatremia.

High-yield Hypernatremia classification recall:

  • Hypovolemic: diuretics, GI losses, burns

  • Euvolemic: diabetes insipidus

  • Hypervolemic: excessive sodium administration/mineralocorticoid excess

Exam pearl: Euvolemic hypernatremia → think diabetes insipidus.

Medicine 05.question: ২২) Which is a post renal cause of AKI?
Medicine 05.exp:
Ureteric stone is a post-renal cause of acute kidney injury (AKI) because it can obstruct urinary outflow, particularly if the obstruction is bilateral or occurs in a patient with a solitary functioning kidney. Obstruction increases intratubular pressure and reduces the glomerular filtration rate.

  • Cardiac failure → prerenal AKI

  • Blood loss → prerenal AKI due to hypovolemia

  • Dehydration → prerenal AKI

High-yield AKI causes recall:

  • Prerenal: dehydration, hemorrhage, cardiac failure

  • Intrinsic renal: ATN, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis

  • Post-renal: stones, tumors, prostate enlargement, urethral obstruction

Exam pearl: AKI + urinary obstruction → think post-renal cause; ureteric stone is a classic example.

Medicine 05.question: ২৩) Which electrolyte imbalance causes muscle weakness?
Medicine 05.exp:
Hypokalemia commonly causes muscle weakness, fatigue, cramps, and in severe cases, paralysis. Reduced extracellular potassium decreases skeletal muscle excitability and can also cause cardiac arrhythmias.

  • Hyponatremia: primarily causes neurological symptoms such as headache, confusion, and seizures.

  • Hypernatremia: mainly causes neurological manifestations due to cellular dehydration.

  • Hyperkalemia: can cause muscle weakness and paralysis too, but in this classic MCQ context, hypokalemia is the expected answer.

High-yield Hypokalemia recall:

  • Muscle weakness and cramps

  • Paralysis in severe cases

  • Ileus/constipation

  • ECG: flattened T waves, ST depression, prominent U waves

  • Common causes: diuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea

Exam pearl: Hypokalemia → muscle weakness + U waves + arrhythmias.

Medicine 05.question: ২৪) Which is true about acute pyelonephritis?
Medicine 05.exp:
WBC casts are characteristic of acute pyelonephritis, indicating inflammation/infection within the renal tubules and interstitium. Pyuria (increased pus cells) is also common.

  • Pus cells absent → false; pyuria is common.

  • Hematuria always present → false; hematuria may occur but is not always present.

  • Organism in culture never present → false; urine culture commonly identifies the causative organism.

High-yield Acute pyelonephritis recall:

  • Fever, chills, flank pain

  • Costovertebral angle tenderness

  • Pyuria

  • WBC casts

  • Positive urine culture, commonly E. coli

Exam pearl: Pyelonephritis → WBC casts; glomerulonephritis → RBC casts.

Medicine 05.question: ২৫) Which diuretic causes hyperkalemia?
Medicine 05.exp:
Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic and an aldosterone antagonist. It decreases sodium reabsorption while reducing potassium excretion in the distal nephron, which can lead to hyperkalemia.

  • Mannitol → osmotic diuretic

  • Frusemide (furosemide) → loop diuretic; causes hypokalemia

  • Thiazide → causes hypokalemia

  • Spironolactone → potassium-sparing; causes hyperkalemia

High-yield Diuretics electrolyte recall:

  • Loop → ↓ K⁺

  • Thiazide → ↓ K⁺

  • Spironolactone → ↑ K⁺

  • Amiloride/triamterene → ↑ K⁺

Exam pearl: Potassium-sparing diuretic → hyperkalemia; classic example = spironolactone.

Medicine 05.question: ২৬) Which glomerular disease is common in adult?
Medicine 05.exp:
Membranous nephropathy is a classic and common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults. It is characterized by diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane due to subepithelial immune-complex deposition.

  • IgA nephropathy → most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide; typically presents with hematuria.

  • Minimal change disease → most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.

  • FSGS → also an important cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, but in classic exam questions, membranous nephropathy is the expected answer.

High-yield Adult glomerular disease recall:

  • Adult nephrotic syndrome → Membranous nephropathy is a classic cause

  • Children nephrotic syndrome → Minimal change disease

  • Recurrent hematuria → IgA nephropathy

  • FSGS → common nephrotic cause, especially associated with HIV, obesity, and heroin use

Exam pearl: Adult nephrotic syndrome → think membranous nephropathy; child → minimal change disease.

Medicine 05.question: ২৭) Which is the most dangerous complication of hypokalemia?
Medicine 05.exp:
The most dangerous complication of hypokalemia is cardiac arrhythmia, which can be potentially fatal. Hypokalemia alters cardiac membrane excitability and repolarization, predisposing to ventricular and supraventricular arrhythmias.

  • Paralytic ileus → recognized complication of hypokalemia but generally less immediately life-threatening.

  • Metabolic alkalosis → may coexist with or contribute to hypokalemia but is not the most dangerous complication.

  • Delirium → not a typical direct complication of hypokalemia.

High-yield Hypokalemia complication recall:

  • Cardiac arrhythmias

  • Muscle weakness/paralysis

  • Cramps

  • Paralytic ileus

  • ECG: U waves, flattened T waves, ST depression

Exam pearl: Hypokalemia can kill through cardiac arrhythmia.

Medicine 05.question: ২৮) What is the usual duration of antibiotic therapy in upper UTI?
Medicine 05.exp:
Upper urinary tract infection (upper UTI), particularly acute pyelonephritis, generally requires a longer antibiotic course than uncomplicated lower UTI because the infection involves the renal parenchyma. A traditional exam-oriented duration is 7–14 days, depending on the antibiotic, severity, and clinical response.

  • 3 days → commonly used for uncomplicated lower UTI/cystitis with selected antibiotics.

  • 7–10 days → may be appropriate for some regimens.

  • 15 days → usually longer than necessary for uncomplicated upper UTI.

High-yield UTI treatment duration recall:

  • Lower uncomplicated UTI → often short course

  • Upper UTI/pyelonephritis → typically 7–14 days

  • Complicated UTI → duration depends on the cause and clinical response

Exam pearl: Upper UTI → think longer treatment, classically 7–14 days.

Medicine 05.question: ২৯) Signs of atropinization excludes......?
Medicine 05.exp:
Atropinization is the therapeutic endpoint when treating organophosphorus compound (OPC) poisoning. Atropine blocks muscarinic effects, producing drying of secretions, mydriasis, tachycardia, and anhidrosis.

Therefore, bradycardia is not a sign of atropinization; atropine typically produces tachycardia.

High-yield Atropinization recall:

  • Dry mouth and dry bronchial secretions

  • Mydriasis

  • Tachycardia

  • Anhidrosis

  • Clear chest with improved bronchial secretions

Exam pearl: Atropinization → dry + dilated pupils + tachycardia; bradycardia is not an endpoint.

Medicine 05.question: ৩০) Which drug is used to shift potassium into cells in hyperkalemia?
Medicine 05.exp:
Salbutamol (albuterol) is a β₂-adrenergic agonist that stimulates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, shifting potassium from the extracellular fluid into cells and temporarily lowering serum potassium.

  • Calcium gluconate → stabilizes the cardiac membrane; does not lower serum K⁺.

  • Frusemide (furosemide) → increases renal potassium excretion.

  • Resonium (sodium polystyrene sulfonate) → removes potassium through the gastrointestinal tract.

High-yield Hyperkalemia management recall:

  • Shift K⁺ into cells: IV insulin + glucose, nebulized salbutamol, sodium bicarbonate in selected cases

  • Stabilize myocardium: IV calcium gluconate

  • Remove K⁺: diuretics, potassium binders, dialysis

Exam pearl: Hyperkalemia + shift K⁺ intracellularly → insulin/glucose or salbutamol.

Medicine 05.question: ৩১) Which is not a feature of Nephrotic syndrome?
Medicine 05.exp:
Hematuria is not a typical feature of nephrotic syndrome; it is more characteristic of nephritic syndromes. Nephrotic syndrome is primarily characterized by massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, generalized edema, and hyperlipidemia.

  • Normal C3: Common in most primary nephrotic syndromes.

  • Massive proteinuria: Cardinal feature.

  • Relapse common: Particularly characteristic of minimal change disease.

High-yield Nephrotic syndrome recall:

  • Massive proteinuria

  • Hypoalbuminemia

  • Generalized edema

  • Hyperlipidemia

  • Lipiduria

  • C3 is usually normal

Exam pearl: Nephrotic = proteinuria + edema; nephritic = hematuria + hypertension + renal impairment.

Medicine 05.question: ৩২) Presence of organism in urine on culture, but no symptom is called.....?
Medicine 05.exp:
Asymptomatic bacteriuria means the presence of significant bacteria in the urine without signs or symptoms of UTI. It is diagnosed by urine culture.

  • Sterile pyuria: White blood cells in urine without significant bacterial growth on routine culture.

  • Significant bacteriuria: Refers to a significant quantity of bacteria in urine, but does not necessarily imply absence of symptoms.

  • Pyelonephritis: Infection of the kidney, usually associated with fever, flank pain, and urinary symptoms.

High-yield UTI recall:

  • Bacteria + no symptoms → asymptomatic bacteriuria

  • Bacteria + urinary symptoms → symptomatic UTI

  • Pyuria + negative routine culture → sterile pyuria

Exam pearl: Positive urine culture + no UTI symptoms = asymptomatic bacteriuria.

Medicine 05.question: ৩৩) Dilated pupil is found in which poisoning?
Medicine 05.exp:
Tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) poisoning causes mydriasis (dilated pupils) due to its anticholinergic effect. Other classic features include dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention, hyperthermia, and altered mental status.

  • OPC poisoning → miosis due to muscarinic excess.

  • Opioid poisoning → pinpoint pupils (miosis).

  • Clonidine poisoning → typically miosis, bradycardia, and hypotension.

High-yield Poisoning pupil findings recall:

  • TCA → mydriasis

  • OPC → miosis

  • Opioids → pinpoint pupils

  • Clonidine → miosis

Exam pearl: TCA poisoning → “anticholinergic” picture → dry + hot + tachycardia + dilated pupils.

Medicine 05.question: ৩৪) What is the ECG change of hypocalcemia?
Medicine 05.exp:
Hypocalcemia characteristically causes prolongation of the QT interval, mainly due to prolongation of the ST segment. Severe hypocalcemia can predispose to ventricular arrhythmias.

  • ST elevation → suggests acute myocardial injury/pericarditis, not a typical feature of hypocalcemia.

  • T-wave inversion → nonspecific and not characteristic.

  • Tall T waves → classically associated with hyperkalemia.

High-yield Hypocalcemia ECG recall:

  • Prolonged QT interval

  • Mainly due to prolonged ST segment

  • Severe cases → risk of ventricular arrhythmias

Exam pearl: Hypocalcemia → prolonged QT; hypercalcemia → shortened QT.

Medicine 05.question: ৩৫) Which antibiotics can be used safely in pregnancy with UTI?
Medicine 05.exp:
Penicillins are generally considered safe for treating UTI during pregnancy. Common choices include amoxicillin or ampicillin, depending on local resistance patterns and culture sensitivity.

  • Tetracyclines → avoided because they can affect fetal teeth and bone development.

  • Trimethoprim → generally avoided in the first trimester because of folate antagonism and risk of neural tube defects.

  • Quinolones → generally avoided during pregnancy because of concerns regarding fetal cartilage/joint development.

High-yield Antibiotics in pregnancy recall:

  • Generally safe: Penicillins, cephalosporins

  • Avoid: Tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones

  • Trimethoprim: avoid particularly in the first trimester

Exam pearl: Pregnancy + UTI → penicillins/cephalosporins are commonly used safe options.

Medicine 05.question: ৩৬) What is the commonest cause of AGN?
Medicine 05.exp:
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is the classic and most common cause of acute glomerulonephritis (AGN), particularly in children. It usually occurs 1–3 weeks after infection with nephritogenic strains of Streptococcus pyogenes, commonly following pharyngitis or impetigo.

Typical presentation includes hematuria, edema, hypertension, oliguria, and reduced complement C3.

High-yield AGN recall:

  • Commonest cause → PSGN

  • Preceding infection → Streptococcus pyogenes

  • Latent period → 1–3 weeks

  • C3 → low, usually returns to normal within weeks

  • Urine → RBC casts, dysmorphic RBCs

Exam pearl: AGN + recent sore throat/skin infection + low C3 → think PSGN.

Medicine 05.question: ৩৭) What is the cause of increased anion gap metabolic acidosis due to exogenous acid load?
Medicine 05.exp:
Aspirin (salicylate) poisoning causes an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis due to accumulation of organic acids and salicylate metabolites. It also characteristically causes a mixed acid–base disorder, with respiratory alkalosis occurring early due to direct stimulation of the respiratory center.

The other options are endogenous causes:

  • DKA → ketoacid accumulation

  • Starvation ketosis → ketone-body accumulation

  • Lactic acidosis → lactate accumulation

High-yield Anion gap metabolic acidosis recall:
A useful mnemonic is GOLD MARK:

  • Glycols

  • Oxoproline

  • L-lactate

  • D-lactate

  • Methanol

  • Aspirin

  • Renal failure

  • Ketoacidosis

Exam pearl: Exogenous acid load + high anion gap → think salicylate (aspirin) poisoning.

Medicine 05.question: ৩৮) Which is not a feature of AGN?
Medicine 05.exp:
Relapse is not a typical feature of acute glomerulonephritis (AGN). AGN, particularly post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, is usually a self-limiting acute condition with hematuria, edema, hypertension, oliguria, and “smoky/cola-colored” urine.

  • Hematuria → common

  • Hypertension → common due to sodium and water retention

  • High/cola-colored urine → due to glomerular hematuria

  • Relapse common → not typical of AGN

High-yield AGN recall:

  • Hematuria

  • Cola/smoky-colored urine

  • Edema

  • Hypertension

  • Oliguria

  • RBC casts

  • Low C3 in PSGN

Exam pearl: AGN is usually self-limiting; recurrent/relapsing disease is not a classic feature.

Medicine 05.question: ৩৯) What is the common complication of respiratory acidosis?
Medicine 05.exp:
Respiratory acidosis occurs when alveolar ventilation is inadequate, causing CO₂ retention (hypercapnia). Therefore, it is classically associated with type-2 (hypercapnic) respiratory failure, characterized by PaCO₂ >6.0 kPa (45 mmHg), often with hypoxemia.

  • Type-1 respiratory failure → primarily hypoxemic, with normal/low PaCO₂.

  • CCF → may cause respiratory failure but is not itself a complication of respiratory acidosis.

  • Pneumothorax → can cause respiratory compromise but is not a complication of respiratory acidosis.

High-yield Respiratory failure recall:

  • Type 1: Low PaO₂, normal/low PaCO₂ → hypoxemic

  • Type 2: Low PaO₂ + high PaCO₂ → hypercapnic

  • Causes of type 2 → COPD, severe asthma, CNS depression, neuromuscular weakness

Exam pearl: Respiratory acidosis = CO₂ retention → think type-2 respiratory failure.

Medicine 05.question: ৪০) Which is antidote for opioids poisoning?
Medicine 05.exp:
Naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist and the first-line antidote for significant opioid poisoning, especially when there is respiratory depression. It rapidly reverses opioid-induced CNS and respiratory depression.

  • Pralidoxime → organophosphorus poisoning

  • Dimercaprol → selected heavy-metal poisonings

  • Flumazenil → benzodiazepine poisoning

High-yield Antidotes recall:

  • Opioids → Naloxone

  • Benzodiazepines → Flumazenil

  • Paracetamol → N-acetylcysteine

  • Organophosphates → Atropine + Pralidoxime

Exam pearl: Opioid poisoning + respiratory depression → Naloxone.

Medicine 05.question: ৪১) Which is not included in general treatment plan of Nephrotic syndrome?
Medicine 05.exp:
Routine protein restriction is not recommended in nephrotic syndrome. Patients have significant urinary protein loss, so an adequate dietary protein intake is generally maintained rather than severely restricted. Excessive protein intake, however, should be avoided.

General supportive treatment includes salt restriction, fluid restriction when significant edema or fluid overload is present, and diuretics for edema.

  • Fluid restriction → may be required in significant edema/hyponatremia.

  • Salt restriction → helps control edema.

  • Diuretics → used to reduce edema.

  • Protein restriction → not a routine component of treatment.

High-yield Nephrotic syndrome treatment recall:

  • Salt restriction

  • Fluid restriction when indicated

  • Diuretics for edema

  • ACE inhibitor/ARB to reduce proteinuria when appropriate

  • Treat the underlying cause

Exam pearl: Nephrotic syndrome → restrict salt, not protein routinely.

Medicine 05.question: ৪২) Which is not a feature of lower UTI?
Medicine 05.exp:
Loin pain is not a typical feature of lower UTI. It suggests involvement of the upper urinary tract, particularly acute pyelonephritis.

Typical lower UTI symptoms include:

  • Dysuria → painful/burning urination

  • Frequency → frequent urination

  • Urgency → sudden compelling need to urinate

High-yield UTI localization recall:

  • Lower UTI: dysuria + frequency + urgency + suprapubic discomfort

  • Upper UTI/pyelonephritis: fever + loin/flank pain + renal angle tenderness

Exam pearl: Dysuria + frequency + urgency = lower UTI; fever + loin pain = upper UTI.

Medicine 05.question: ৪৩) Which poisoning is common in children?
Medicine 05.exp:
Kerosene poisoning is a common accidental poisoning in children, particularly in areas where kerosene is stored in easily accessible containers. Children may ingest it accidentally because of its appearance and availability.

The major danger is aspiration into the lungs, which can cause chemical pneumonitis. Therefore, inducing vomiting or routine gastric lavage is generally avoided because it increases aspiration risk.

High-yield Pediatric poisoning recall:

  • Kerosene → common accidental poisoning in children

  • Major complication → aspiration pneumonitis

  • Avoid inducing vomiting

  • Supportive treatment is the mainstay

Exam pearl: Child + hydrocarbon ingestion → think kerosene; biggest risk = aspiration pneumonitis.

Medicine 05.question: ৪৪) If tetany is not corrected by calcium gluconate then what can be used?
Medicine 05.exp:
If tetany due to hypocalcemia does not respond adequately to calcium gluconate, magnesium replacement should be considered because hypomagnesemia can cause or worsen hypocalcemia and make it resistant to calcium therapy. Magnesium sulphate is therefore used when magnesium deficiency is suspected or confirmed.

High-yield Tetany recall:

  • Common cause → hypocalcemia

  • Initial treatment → IV calcium gluconate

  • Refractory hypocalcemia/tetany → check and correct Mg²⁺ deficiency

  • Severe hypomagnesemia can impair PTH secretion and action.

Exam pearl: Tetany not responding to calcium → think hypomagnesemia → give magnesium.

Medicine 05.question: ৪৫) Which is neurotoxic sign in snake bite patient?
Medicine 05.exp:
“Broken neck sign” is a neurotoxic manifestation of snake envenomation, particularly seen with cobra and krait bites. It results from progressive neuromuscular paralysis, causing neck muscle weakness and inability to hold the head upright.

  • Respiratory failure → can occur as a severe consequence of neurotoxicity, but the specific neurotoxic sign here is broken neck sign.

  • Bleeding → indicates hemotoxic/vasculotoxic envenomation.

  • Renal shutdown → suggests nephrotoxicity or severe systemic envenomation.

High-yield Snake bite neurotoxicity recall:

  • Ptosis

  • Diplopia

  • Dysphagia

  • Dysarthria

  • Broken neck sign

  • Progressive respiratory muscle paralysis

Exam pearl: Snake bite + ptosis + broken neck sign → neurotoxic envenomation (cobra/krait).

Medicine 05.question: ৪৬) What is absolute contraindication of stomach wash?
Medicine 05.exp:
Corrosive poisoning (strong acids or alkalis) is an absolute contraindication to gastric lavage/stomach wash because passing a tube and inducing lavage can cause further injury, perforation, and aspiration of the corrosive material.

  • OPC poisoning: Gastric lavage may be considered in selected early cases with a protected airway.

  • Sedative poisoning: May be considered in selected severe, early cases with airway protection.

  • Arsenic poisoning: Gastric decontamination may be considered depending on timing and circumstances.

High-yield Gastric lavage contraindications recall:

  • Corrosive ingestion

  • Hydrocarbon ingestion with high aspiration risk

  • Unprotected airway in a patient with impaired consciousness

Exam pearl: Corrosive poisoning → never perform gastric lavage.

Medicine 05.question: ৪৭) Which one is called street poisoning?
Medicine 05.exp:
Datura poisoning is classically known as “street poisoning” because criminals may use Datura-containing substances to incapacitate or disorient victims and facilitate robbery or other crimes. Datura contains atropine-like anticholinergic alkaloids, mainly atropine and scopolamine.

Typical features include mydriasis, dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention, hyperthermia, delirium, and hallucinations.

High-yield Datura poisoning recall:

  • Also called street poisoning

  • Anticholinergic toxicity

  • “Dry as a bone, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter”

  • Mydriasis + dry mouth + tachycardia + delirium

Exam pearl: Street poisoning = Datura → anticholinergic syndrome

Medicine 05.question: ৪৮) What is the minimum amount of fluid to be taken for prophylaxis of recurrent UTI?
Medicine 05.exp:
Adequate fluid intake helps prevent recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) by increasing urine production and promoting regular flushing of bacteria from the urinary tract. A commonly taught target is at least 2 litres of fluid per day, unless medically contraindicated.

High-yield Recurrent UTI prevention recall:

  • Adequate hydration → aim for ≥2 L/day

  • Regular and complete bladder emptying

  • Avoid delaying urination

  • Post-coital urination may help reduce recurrence in susceptible women

Exam pearl: Recurrent UTI prophylaxis → maintain adequate hydration, commonly ≥2 L/day.

Medicine 05.question: ৪৯) What is the number of total snake species in Bangladesh?
Medicine 05.exp:
According to the traditional exam-oriented classification, Bangladesh is commonly stated to have approximately 98 species of snakes. This figure includes both venomous and non-venomous species.

High-yield Snake bite recall:

  • Total snake species in Bangladesh → 98 (classic exam figure)

  • Medically important venomous snakes include cobra, krait, Russell's viper, and green pit viper.

Exam pearl: Bangladesh → 98 snake species (traditional exam figure).

Medicine 05.question: ৫০) Absence of remission despite therapy with 4 weeks of daily prednisolone in a dose of 2 mg/kg/day is called....... NS?
Medicine 05.exp:
In childhood nephrotic syndrome, failure to achieve remission after 4 weeks of daily prednisolone at 2 mg/kg/day is classically defined as steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome.

  • Complete remission: Proteinuria disappears with treatment.

  • Frequent relapse: ≥2 relapses within 6 months or ≥4 relapses within 12 months.

  • Steroid-dependent: Relapse occurs during steroid therapy or shortly after stopping it.

  • Steroid-resistant: No remission after the standard initial steroid course.

High-yield Nephrotic syndrome recall:

  • 4 weeks prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day + no remission → steroid-resistant

  • Frequent relapse → ≥2 relapses/6 months or ≥4 relapses/12 months

  • Steroid-dependent → relapse during taper/within 2 weeks of stopping steroids

Exam pearl: No remission after 4 weeks of adequate prednisolone → SRNS.
